title: The Idea That Redlined a Nation
voiceover: Most of the harm in this story did not start with a mob. It started with a number. In 1933 the University of Chicago Press published a thick book called One Hundred Years of Land Values in Chicago. The author was an economist named Homer Hoyt, and the book had begun as his doctoral dissertation here at the University of Chicago. It runs more than five hundred pages. It tracks the price of Chicago dirt, block by block, from 1830 to 1933. Hoyt was a careful man with numbers. He had a law degree and a doctorate, and he could read a city the way a doctor reads an x ray. Most of the book is dry, page after page of tables and curves. One table is not. In that table Hoyt ranked races and nationalities by their supposed effect on land values. At the top he put English, Germans, Scots, Irish, and Scandinavians. Below them, North Italians. Then Bohemians, Poles, Lithuanians, Greeks. Near the bottom he placed Russian Jews of the lower class and South Italians. At the very bottom he wrote Negroes, and then Mexicans. Hoyt added a note that mattered. The other groups, he wrote, would blend in once they rose in income and lived like Americans. For Black and Mexican residents, he said, that door stayed closed. He had taken an old prejudice and dressed it as economics. The table did not read like hate. It read like a footnote, calm and precise, which is exactly what made it dangerous. A banker could cite it. A judge could cite it. An appraiser could fold it into a formula and never feel the cruelty of it. This did not come from nowhere. The University of Chicago was the home of a famous school of urban sociology. Robert Park and Ernest Burgess borrowed words from plant biology to describe city neighborhoods. They wrote about invasion and succession, as if a Black family moving onto a block were a species pushing out another. The language made segregation sound like a law of nature instead of a choice people made. Hoyt took that frame and gave it a dollar sign. A neighborhood, he argued, lost value the moment certain people arrived. He never quite asked the obvious question. Did the value fall because Black families moved in, or because white owners and white banks decided it should, and pulled their money out to make it true. He measured the wound and called it weather. So far this was a theory in a book. Then the federal government hired the man who wrote it. In 1934 Congress created the Federal Housing Administration to insure home loans and pull the country out of the Depression. The FHA needed rules. It needed to decide which mortgages were safe to back. Homer Hoyt became its chief land economist. The agency also leaned on Frederick Babcock, an appraiser who had written that the presence of what he called inharmonious racial groups dragged values down. The two of them helped write the FHA Underwriting Manual. That manual was not a private opinion. It was a federal instruction book sent to lenders across the nation. Read the 1938 edition and the logic is plain. It tells appraisers to study whether incompatible racial groups are present near a property. It praises natural or artificial barriers, a river, a wide road, a park, that could keep a neighborhood, in its words, protected from adverse influences. It openly recommends a deed clause barring the wrong people, and gives that clause extra points. The prejudice Hoyt charted in 1933 was now a checklist a bank used to say yes or no. Think about the scale of that. The FHA would go on to insure tens of billions of dollars in home loans over the following decades, and that wealth built the American middle class one mortgage at a time. The manual decided who got in line for it. A white family in a quiet suburb was a safe bet. A Black family on the South Side was a hazard by definition, whatever their savings or their record. The subsidy flowed one way, and a generation of equity piled up on one side of the line. Around the same time, another New Deal agency drew the idea onto maps. The Home Owners Loan Corporation had been set up to refinance failing mortgages. From 1935 to 1940 it ran a survey of American cities and produced about two hundred and thirty nine color coded maps. Surveyors graded each neighborhood. Green was A, the best. Blue was B. Yellow was C. Red was D, hazardous, the lowest grade. The notes the surveyors wrote down explain the colors. A green area was native born and well off. A red area was old, crowded, or, again and again in the margins, home to Negro families or what one writer called an infiltration of them. On the Chicago maps, the Black Belt on the South Side was washed in red. The grade was not really about the houses. It was about who lived inside them. The word redlining comes from that red ink. A family in a red zone could not get a federally backed loan no matter how steady their paycheck was. They could not buy. They often could not borrow to repair. So the houses aged, and rents stayed high because there was nowhere else to go, and absentee landlords carved single homes into a dozen kitchenettes. Then a new surveyor would arrive, see the crowding the redline had caused, and grade the block hazardous all over again. The map became a wall, and the wall became real. This was not a Chicago story for long. Those maps covered cities in nearly every corner of the country, from Atlanta to Los Angeles, from Boston to Birmingham. An idea worked out in a Hyde Park seminar room had been turned into a national machine. And while the federal government drew its lines, private owners built their own. The favorite tool was the racially restrictive covenant, a clause written into a deed promising that the property would never be sold or rented to Black residents, and sometimes to Asians or Jews. In Chicago whole subdivisions signed them, block clubs went door to door collecting names, and the University of Chicago itself quietly bankrolled the defense of covenants in the neighborhoods around its campus. From 1933 to 1947 the University spent more than eighty three thousand dollars protecting them. The covenant and the redline worked as a pair. One kept the money out. The other kept the people out. Together they held the South Side Black Belt in place like a clamp. Which brings us back to one block. In the spring of 1937 a Black real estate broker named Carl Hansberry bought a three flat at 6140 South Rhodes Avenue, just south of Washington Park. He moved his family in on June the fifteenth. That night two bricks came through the front window. His wife, Nannie, took to patrolling the house with a loaded pistol while the children slept. One of those children was eight year old Lorraine Hansberry, who would grow up to write A Raisin in the Sun. Years later she remembered that brick coming through the glass, missing her by inches, and she remembered her mother walking the rooms at night with the gun. The Washington Park subdivision was covered by a covenant barring Black occupants, and within days six of the new neighbors filed suit to force the family out. Hansberry did not move out. He sued. His lawyers found a crack in the paper. The covenant was supposed to take effect only if the owners of ninety five percent of the frontage signed it, and in truth far fewer had. The case reached the Supreme Court in 1940 as Hansberry versus Lee. Hansberry won, but on narrow ground. The Court did not say covenants were illegal. It said this particular one had not been properly approved and could not bind him. The wall had a gap in it. The wall itself still stood. It took eight more years to shake it. The decisive case came from St. Louis. In 1945 a Black family named Shelley bought a home on Labadie Avenue, not knowing a covenant from 1911 forbade it. A neighbor named Kraemer, who lived blocks away, sued to throw them out. A nearly identical fight was unfolding in Detroit, where the McGhee family faced a covenant of its own. Thurgood Marshall and Loren Miller argued for the families. On the third of May, 1948, the Supreme Court ruled in Shelley versus Kraemer. The decision was clever and limited at once. A covenant between private people, the Court said, was not itself against the Constitution. But the moment a court enforced one, the government became the enforcer, and the Fourteenth Amendment forbids the government from discriminating that way. So the clauses could no longer be enforced. It was a real victory, and Black families across the country began to cross the old lines. But notice what the Court did not do. It did not strike the covenants from the deeds. It did not ban redlining. It did not touch the FHA manual. It pulled one tool out of the toolbox and left the rest on the bench. They could still be written. And they were. For years afterward the racist language sat in millions of American deeds, including thousands here in Chicago, legally dead but never erased. You can still order a copy of your deed today and find it there, a sentence that no longer has teeth but never had to apologize. Illinois did not let homeowners formally strike that language from the record until well into our own century. And the lines drawn in the 1930s did not fade when the law changed. Researchers who lay the old HOLC maps over the cities of today find the red zones still poorer, still sicker, still hotter in summer, with less tree cover and shorter lives. The wall came down. The shadow it cast did not. That is the shape of this harm. It rarely shouted. It was a table in a book, a manual in a file drawer, a color on a map, a line in a deed. Quiet, official, and built to last.
